A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PETRA, and their text, equations, tables and figures support a reliable comparison. v1 ends with references; v2 adds Appendices A and B. Retained material can be matched despite formatting changes.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification experiments on CIFAR-10, ImageNet32 and ImageNet, including accuracy results in Table 2 and an accumulation-factor experiment in Figure 4.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds CIFAR-100 ablations, distributed timing measurements, stage memory measurements and gradient diagnostics in its appendices.

M1.justification: The PETRA procedure in Equation 5 and Algorithm 1 is unchanged: asynchronous stages reconstruct activations using current parameters, accumulate gradients and retain input buffers for non-reversible stages. The new buffer variants are experimental controls, not revisions to PETRA.

E1.justification: v2 adds CIFAR-100 classification for the buffer ablation in Table 4. CIFAR-10, ImageNet32 and ImageNet remain covered; the new timing and gradient analyses otherwise use retained datasets and tasks.

E2.justification: Table 2 retains its comparator set. Table 4 newly compares accuracy against buffered delayed gradients and variants retaining different buffers, while Appendix B directly compares PETRA gradients with standard delayed gradients and end-to-end backpropagation gradients.

E3.justification: The original classification protocol is retained, but v2 introduces substantial new evaluation procedures: buffer ablations with k=1, timing with micro-batches of 256 on 10 or 18 GPUs after 500 warm-up iterations, and layerwise gradient diagnostics during training. These are added protocols, not evidence that the retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Table 4 adds controlled tests separating gradient delay, parameter buffering and activation reconstruction. Appendix A examines memory by stage, and Appendix B studies gradient alignment and norm ratios across depth and training. These directly investigate PETRA's approximations beyond the retained accumulation analysis.

E5.justification: v2 adds explicit aggregation procedures for new measurements: timing averages over 50 mini-batches and gradient diagnostics averaged over 15 measurements per epoch, then smoothed with a rolling window of 10. The existing three-run CIFAR-10 averages and variance-below-0.1 statement remain unchanged; no additional independent-run counts or confidence intervals are reported.

E6.justification: Tables 2–3 and Figure 4 retain their results. New Table 4 reports CIFAR-100 PETRA accuracies of 75.9, 75.2 and 77.2 for RevNet-18/34/50. Table 5 reports PETRA versus reversible-backpropagation times of 53.4 versus 160.3 ms and 97.1 versus 235.6 ms, yielding 3.0× and 2.4× speedups. Appendices add stage memory and gradient-quality results.

T1.justification: The main mathematical formulation, Equations 1–5 and the idealized complexity comparison remain unchanged. Appendix B explains the existing delay and approximation mechanism and supplies standard diagnostic formulas, without a substantive new derivation, theorem or proof.

C1.justification: v2 adds an explicit numbered contribution claiming an observed empirical throughput increase. The central claims about reversible reconstruction, eliminating buffers at reversible stages, parallel training and competitive classification accuracy otherwise retain their meaning.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of why approximation quality varies with depth, learning-rate reductions and convergence. Appendix B argues that using current weights can improve alignment with end-to-end gradients relative to standard delayed gradients. Section 4.2 also interprets the buffer ablations and discusses stage imbalance when assessing throughput.

D1.justification: v2 documents deployment across 10 or 18 GPUs, timing warm-up and measurement counts, and diagnostic sampling and non-reversible stage indices. It also updates the PETRA repository address. The optimizer recipe, architectural adaptations and single-A100 memory specification are retained.

R1.justification: The cited works and related-work positioning remain the same, including the relationships to reversible networks, pipeline parallelism and delayed gradients. Author-year citations and expanded bibliographic metadata do not introduce new research positioning.

P1.justification: The main section order and most existing prose are retained. v2 makes localized explanatory rewrites, extends Section 4.2, adds appendix headings, and updates the title, affiliations, acknowledgments and citation style. This is not an extensive rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 4–6 and two multipanel figures, substantially expanding the visual presentation. It also adopts the ICLR layout and resizes existing displays. New presentation defects include Figure 5b showing norm ratios under a cosine-similarity caption and conflicting epoch labels in Figure 6.

improvement.justification: v1 supported its efficiency argument mainly through idealized complexity and memory estimates. v2 adds actual distributed timing in Table 5 and controlled tests of its approximation choices in Table 4 and Appendix B, addressing important validation gaps. The timing comparison remains limited to basic model parallelism, and Figures 5–6 contain reporting inconsistencies, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in empirical support.
